title: The Books: how the magical alphabets passed from hand to hand
summary: The magical alphabets reached the modern world through a short chain of books. Trithemius's Polygraphia (July 1518) printed the Theban in its sixth book, ascribing it to Honorius of Thebes. Abraham de Balmes's Hebrew grammar (Venice, 1523) printed what Macfarlane (2025) calls the first ring-letter alphabet printed in Europe. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (July 1533) gathered the Theban and three Hebrew-keyed alphabets into a working handbook. Re-cut, its tables reached later readers through the English of 1651 and Barrett's Magus (1801). Beside that chain ran the compendia of the world's alphabets: Postel 1538; Ambrogio 1539, the earliest known printing of the so-called Alphabet of the Magi; Vigenère 1586; Duret 1613; Kircher 1652–79. They set the magical alphabets beside real scripts. The revival of Lévi, Paul Christian and the Golden Dawn (1854–1888 and after) put them back to use.

firstAttestation.work: Polygraphiae libri sex Ioannis Trithemij, abbatis Peapolitani quondam Spanheimensis, ad Maximilianum Caesarem (title as in the Library of Congress record)
firstAttestation.author: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), abbot of Sponheim and, from October 1506, of St Jakob at Würzburg (prefatory life in the 1518 print, OCR of the Wellcome copy); printed after his death
firstAttestation.date: July 1518. Two colophon transcriptions are reported. The Library of Congress gives 'Impressum ductu Ioannis Haselberg de Aia biblipolae, anno a Christo nato MDXVIII men. Iulio', from leaf C4 verso. The Folger gives 'impressum aere ac impensis integerrimi bibliopolae Ioannis Haselbergi de Aia Constantiensis Dioecesis, anno MDXVIII mense Iulio'. UVaDoc says both parts carry colophons and takes its data from the second, on C3v. The text is older than the print. In the Wellcome copy's OCR the end of Book IV is dated 13 March 1508 (OCR, garbled: 'xírj. die Martrj, anno M. D. V HT') and the end of Book V 'Anno domini M. D. VIII'. Neither date was checked on the page images.
firstAttestation.place: Basel or Oppenheim. The Library of Congress gives '[Basel]', taking the place from VD16 (T 1994). The Wellcome copy's Internet Archive record gives '[Basle]: A. Petri for J. Haselberger de Aia', and the Met names Adam Petri as printer. The Folger queries Basel and names Michael Furter and Adam Petri as associated names; per the theban fact-check, it also notes that Furter died in 1517. Christie's and older repertories give Oppenheim (Köbel). The colophon names the bookseller Johannes Haselberg of Aia, who paid for the printing ('aere ac impensis', Folger).
firstAttestation.locator: Book VI. Seen in the Wellcome copy (Internet Archive b33552137; OCR, and page images of leaves 504–506). Book V closes 'quintum quoque Polygraphiae librum terminamus. Anno domini M. D. VIII'. The passage before the Theban speaks of 'huius libri sexti'. Book VI closes 'Finis libri sexti Polygraphiae'. The sentence introducing the Theban stands at the foot of a recto, and the table heads the next verso. This is about sig. ²q5r–v, inferred from a signature that the OCR reads as 'q iiii' two pages earlier; no signature was seen on an image. The printing is unpaginated (LoC '[540] p.'; Wellcome '256 unnumbered leaves'), so Peterson's 'p. 579' and Wikipedia's 'p. 597' must be pages of a later edition.
firstAttestation.notes: The earliest printed book in the lineage that this research documents, and the earliest printed home of a magical alphabet found (the Theban). The ascription to Honorius, on Pietro d'Abano's testimony, is Trithemius's; it is not a fact about the alphabet's origin. Not excluded: the theban fact-check reports that Trithemius gave Maximilian a manuscript version in 1508 (ed. Gamer, Brill 2022). That manuscript may already hold the table; it was not checked. The first printed ring-letter alphabet followed in 1523 (de Balmes; Macfarlane 2025). Behind both stand manuscripts: the charaktêres of ancient magic, the medieval Jewish ring-letter alphabets, and Agrippa's draft of 1509–10, whose contents regarding the alphabets are not established.

They stand on pp. CCLXXIII (misprinted 'CCXLXXIII') and CCLXXIIII in the LoC and McGill copies. II.22 has the planetary tables; II.48 and II.51 the geomantic figures and characters. The main route into later use. [checked in the 1533 print]

claims.claim: Honorius of Thebes devised the Theban alphabet.
claims.evidence: Trithemius (1518, Book VI) introduces 'aliud alphabetum Honorij cognomento Thebani', which Honorius used to hide 'suas in magicis fatuitates', 'sicut Petrus de Apono testatur in suo maiore libro quarto' (checked against the Wellcome copy). Peterson could not find such a passage in d'Abano (via the theban fact-check). The only Honorius manuscript that carries the alphabet, the composite BL Sloane 3853, names Agrippa as its source (Peterson; Wikipedia, in search results). No copy earlier than 1518 is known; the 1508 manuscript version of the Polygraphia (Gamer 2022) was not checked. Write: 'Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius of Thebes'.
sources: Peterson, introduction to The Sworn Book of Honorius

claims.claim: Agrippa took the Theban from Trithemius.
claims.evidence: Agrippa III.29 (1533) reads 'quos notat Petrus Apponus ab Honorio Thebano traditos' (LoC copy, checked), fifteen years after the Polygraphia. In 1651: 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes' (p. 438, checked). Agrippa does not name Trithemius here. The dependence is an inference from the agreement of the texts and the documented contact of 1509–10, and it is drawn by modern editors (Peterson's annotation). It is not Agrippa's statement.

claims.claim: Agrippa invented the Celestial, the Malachim and the Passing of the River.
claims.evidence: Against: Agrippa opens III.30 'Apud Hebreos plures characterum inuenio modos' (1533, checked); J.F. 1651: 'Amongst the Hebrews I finde more fashions of Characters' (p. 439, checked). The chapter heading gives the matter as 'à Cabalistis traditus' ('delivered by Cabalists'). The River script was printed by de Balmes (1523) and Panteo (1530) before him, and ring-letter alphabets keyed to Hebrew stand in medieval Jewish manuscripts (Bohak 2011; Macfarlane 2025). His book is the main route by which they reached later readers, which is why his name is attached to them.

claims.claim: De Balmes's grammar (Venice, 1523) printed the first ring-letter alphabet in Europe.
claims.evidence: Macfarlane (JHI 86.3, 2025, 473–506), as shown in search summaries of the Project MUSE page, describes de Balmes's 1523 grammar as the first place an alphabet of Brillenbuchstaben was printed in Europe. This is a paraphrase; her wording was not seen in full. Peterson's note and Wikipedia give sig. B6v; the page itself was not seen.

claims.claim: The River script is the writing Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates.
claims.evidence: Panteo (1530) is the first known to assign it to Abraham (Macfarlane, following Campanini). Blavatsky (1892) offers another river, the Chebar of Ezekiel. The Hebrew name ever ha-nahar, 'beyond the River', has a Talmudic background that Christian readers did not know (Campanini).

claims.claim: The Celestial alphabet is read from the stars.
claims.evidence: Agrippa III.30 says the Celestial is so called 'quia inter sydera collocatam & figuratam ostendunt' (1533, checked); J.F. 1651: 'because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars' (p. 439, checked). But in II.51 he calls the Malachim 'the true Characters of the heavens' (1651, p. 316; 1533: 'Veri autem characteres coelorum, ipsa est scriptura angelorum, quae apud Hebraeos vocatur scriptura Malachim'), so star-writing is not his claim for the Celestial alone. Postel (1538, per Peter Harrington's description) and Gaffarel (1629) built star-letter theories; Macfarlane (2025) gives the history. No source found shows that any Celestial letter matches a constellation.

claims.claim: Agrippa's 1510 draft already contained the alphabets.
claims.evidence: Not established either way. The draft exists (Würzburg UB, M. ch. q. 50, per a search-seen source) and Perrone Compagni's edition (1992) takes account of it; that edition was not consulted. Agrippa's 'To the Reader' (1651, checked) says that for the print 'we added some Chapters, and we inserted many things'. That shows enlargement, not which chapters. The '1510' date sometimes given for the Malachim comes from the draft, not from any sight of the alphabet in it.

claims.claim: The alphabets of Adam, Enoch, Abraham and Moses printed by the compilers are the scripts of the patriarchs.
claims.evidence: [P] Rocca (1591), de Bry (1596) and Duret (1613) print alphabets under these names, as the researcher recalls; not verified. Search-backed in part: Fry (1799) reports Ambrogio's claim that the angel Raphael gave a script to Adam (Wikipedia, 'Alphabet of the Magi'), and Duret reprints it as 'the characters of the angel Raphael'. Such ascriptions record what was believed about the invention of writing.

claims.claim: Theseus Ambrosius printed characters written by a demon at a conjuring by Lodovico de Spoletano (Ludovicus Spoletanus).
claims.evidence: A search summary of a secondary source (not named in the summary) reports that Ambrogio tells of a levitating pen and of a document said to be in a demon's own hand, after the demon was conjured by one Lodovico de Spoletano, which he chose not to study. Whether the 1539 book prints the characters, and whether later compilers copied them as 'diabolical letters', is the researcher's recollection [P]. Report it as the book's story.

claims.claim: Duret took his magical alphabets from Agrippa, Ambrosius and Vigenère.
claims.evidence: [P] As the researcher recalls, Duret names his sources as he goes; not checked in the scan. Search-backed in part: the Lyon library blog says Duret's alphabet of the angel Raphael is taken from Theseus Ambrosius.

claims.claim: The Enochian alphabet was given by angels.
claims.evidence: Dee records it as shown in Kelley's visions, and wrote out his table on 6 May 1583 (Sloane MS 3188, f. 104). Report it as Dee's record.

claims.claim: The Shawq al-mustahām is by Ibn Waḥshiyya.
claims.evidence: Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts the ascription.

claims.claim: Paul Christian first printed the Alphabet of the Magi.
claims.evidence: REFUTED (the schema has no 'refuted' standing). The alphabet was printed by Teseo Ambrogio (Pavia, 1539), Claude Duret (1613) and Edmund Fry (1799), and named 'Alphabet of the Magi' on Mathers's Plate XV (1888/89). Sources: Wikipedia, 'Alphabet of the Magi'; the Lyon library blog; dCode agrees; the search-backed alphabet-of-the-magi fact-check. Paul Christian (1870) is not the first printing, and whether he prints it at all is unverified.

claims.claim: The Golden Dawn's Cipher Manuscripts are written in a cipher taken from Trithemius.
claims.evidence: Search summaries agree that the Cipher Manuscripts are written in a Trithemian substitution cipher (Wikipedia, 'Cipher Manuscripts'). One source names the French Polygraphie (1561) as the source of the script. House data agrees (esoteric.js, themes/latin.js).

claims.claim: Fräulein Anna Sprengel authorised the founding of the Golden Dawn.
claims.evidence: Westcott's account. Ellic Howe (1972) and R. A. Gilbert concluded that Westcott wrote the letters himself; that is the standing view.

claims.claim: Kircher set the ring-letter alphabets inside his history of the Hebrew alphabet.
claims.evidence: Macfarlane (2025), for the Oedipus Aegyptiacus (vol. II, 1653) and Turris Babel (1679).

claims.claim: Most modern charts of the four Agrippan alphabets follow the 1651 English plates or Barrett's 1801 plate, not 1533.
claims.evidence: Not demonstrated. The sibling research shows particular cases: Wikipedia's Malachim table follows 1651, and Westcott's Flying Roll XXXII copies Barrett's plate. The generalisation 'most modern charts' has no survey behind it, and the sibling fact-checks removed it as unverified. Later printings used new cuts or engravings.

claims.claim: Tory's 'Lettres Chaldaïques' (1529) are the River script.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia says Tory labels the alphabet 'Lettres Chaldaiques' at f. 76v (search-seen). The BnF image record (f. 73r) describes them as letters of Moses's time. Not checked against the book.

claims.claim: Panteo's alphabet (1530) is a conglomeration of all three of Agrippa's alphabets.
claims.evidence: Reported second-hand on a blog (Pelling, Cipher Mysteries, 2009). Unchecked.

claims.claim: The 'Vigenère cipher' is Vigenère's invention.
claims.evidence: [P] The square table goes back to Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518); Vigenère's own contribution was an autokey method (Kahn 1967, not consulted). A bookseller's description seen in search says the 1586 book 'includes a definitive form of what became the Vigenère square, inspired by Alberti and Trithemius'. The 1518 book's own index (Wellcome copy OCR) says Book V sets the Latin letters out in two tables, one called 'recta' and the other 'aversa'.

claims.claim: In the 1533 edition the Celestial, Malachim and Passing of the River stand in a single woodcut, in three rows.
claims.evidence: REFUTED (the schema has no 'refuted' standing). In the LoC copy, seen in page images, they are three separately captioned tables. 'Scriptura Coelestis' stands on p. CCLXXIII (misprinted 'CCXLXXIII', signed z iii), with the caption 'Scriptura Malachim' at its foot. The Malachim table and 'Scriptura transitus fluuii' follow on p. CCLXXIIII. The McGill copy's OCR shows the same layout. The single-woodcut idea rests on a stock-image caption. In 1651 they stand on pp. 439, 440 and 441.
sources: Agrippa 1533, LoC copy (Internet Archive DeOccultaPhilosophiaLoc1533), pp. CCLXXIII–CCLXXIIII

claims.claim: The earliest known printing of the so-called Alphabet of the Magi is Teseo Ambrogio's Introductio (Pavia, 1539).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia ('Alphabet of the Magi', citing 'pp. 202f.', probably fol. 202 since the book is foliated) and the Lyon library blog via Duret; Fry (1799) reports Ambrogio as his source. Secondary sources only: the 1539 print was not viewed. The pedigree Ambrogio reports for it (Gamaliel; the Liber ignis; the angel Raphiel, per Wikipedia) is legend.

letters.name: The charaktêres of the Greek magical papyri, curse tablets and gems
letters.value: No alphabet: rows of ring-ended signs (charaktêres) that stand for no letter
letters.translit: Papyri, lead, metal and stone; no single book
letters.form: The prelude, not a book. The Greek magical papyri, the lead curse tablets, the metal lamellae and the engraved gems of the Roman period set rows of signs, many with small rings at the ends of their strokes, beside divine names and voces magicae, to be copied exactly as given. They are not letters and spell nothing. Their line runs on into Jewish amulets of Late Antiquity, Coptic ritual handbooks and the recipe books of the Cairo Genizah, and from there into the medieval ring-letter alphabets keyed to Hebrew (Bohak 2011). Standard edition of the papyri: K. Preisendanz, Papyri Graecae Magicae (1928–31; the 2nd edition by A. Henrichs, 1973–74, is the researcher's recollection, not checked).
letters.note: [S] charakteres.json. That file's own basis for the ancient material is mostly prior knowledge; the Bohak 2011 article is search-backed. Show this as the opening card of the lineage, marked as signs, not an alphabet. FACT-CHECK: the date range is aligned with the search-backed charakteres check (end 700, was 500). Preisendanz's dates were not confirmed by search.
letters.author: anonymous practitioners and scribes
letters.date: Roman imperial period and Late Antiquity. The Rylands blog (Part I) dates the signs from roughly the 2nd–3rd century CE; Dzwiza (2013), via the charakteres fact-check, gives the handbook corpus as 1st–7th century.
letters.place: Egypt for the papyri; the lead tablets, lamellae and gems come from across the Roman world
letters.tookFrom: Not known.
letters.gaveTo: Late Antique Jewish amulets; Coptic handbooks; Genizah recipe books; ultimately the ring-letter alphabets.
letters.dating: Conventional period dating of the corpus; no single object is dated here.

editions.label: Bohak, "The Charaktêres in Ancient and Medieval Jewish Magic" (2011)

letters.name: Shawq al-mustahām, ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya
letters.value: A catalogue of 'ancient', planetary and sages' alphabets, many drawn with ring-ends
letters.form: An Arabic book of the scripts of the ancients. It presents a series of alphabets as the writing of earlier peoples, of the planets and of the sages, many of them drawn with ring-ends, and it has a section on Egyptian hieroglyphs. It survives in manuscript, and its tables were re-copied and varied like other collections of the 'pens' (aqlām) of the sages. It reached European print only in 1806, in Joseph Hammer's London edition with an English version. No link between it and the Hebrew-keyed alphabets of Agrippa is documented.
letters.note: [S] ibn-wahshiyya.json. That file also had no web search and gives no URLs. Keep the ascription as an ascription, and do not say the book deciphered the hieroglyphs. FACT-CHECK: the ibn-wahshiyya research and its own fact-check both ran without web search. Treat every fact on this card as [P].
letters.native: Kitāb Shawq al-mustahām fī maʿrifat rumūz al-aqlām
letters.author: ascribed to Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Waḥshiyya; the ascription is doubted (Hämeen-Anttila 2006)
letters.date: If the ascription holds, about 900–930 CE: his Nabatean Agriculture was dictated in 318 AH / 930–31 CE, according to its transmitter. The date of the earliest surviving manuscript of the Shawq is not established.
letters.place: Iraq is Ibn Waḥshiyya's milieu; where the Shawq itself was written is not known
printed: the alphabets of the ancients, planets and sages (number not established)
letters.tookFrom: It presents itself as a key to the scripts of ancient books. Its actual sources are not established.
letters.gaveTo: Hammer's edition (London, 1806); Okasha El Daly's re-reading of its hieroglyph section (2005).
letters.dating: Depends on the ascription, which Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts.

letters.name: Medieval Jewish magical and kabbalistic manuscripts: the ring-letter alphabets
letters.value: Alphabets of ring-letters (Brillenbuchstaben) keyed one-for-one to the 22 Hebrew letters, as writings of angels
letters.form: In medieval Jewish manuscripts the old signs were set against the Hebrew alphabet: each of the 22 letters was given a ring-ended counterpart, and the whole was treated as the writing of angels. Bohak (2011) follows the signs from Greek into Jewish magic and down to these alphabets. Macfarlane (2025) shows how learned Christians took such Brillenbuchstaben from kabbalistic manuscripts and came to treat them as alphabets derived from the stars and authored by angels. Later Jewish charm books still carry them, for instance British Library Or 10161, fol. 21v.
letters.note: [S] charakteres, celestial, malachim, transitus-fluvii (Macfarlane 2025, abstract and snippets; Bohak 2011; Rylands blog, 2022).
letters.author: anonymous Jewish practitioners and scribes
letters.date: Medieval. The Genizah material runs from about the 10th to the 13th century and later; the kabbalistic manuscripts are later still. No single dated manuscript with such an alphabet is named in this research.
letters.place: The Cairo Genizah; Jewish communities of the Mediterranean and of Europe
printed: Hebrew-keyed ring-letter alphabets (names and number vary)
letters.tookFrom: The charaktêres of Graeco-Egyptian and Late Antique Jewish magic (Bohak 2011).
letters.gaveTo: Abraham de Balmes's printed 'script beyond the River' (1523); the three Hebrew-keyed alphabets of Agrippa III.30 (1533), by a route that is not documented.
letters.dating: Period only. Do not date any one of the printed alphabets to a medieval manuscript without a shelfmark.

editions.label: Rylands blog, "Speaking to angels", Part I (2022)

letters.name: Agrippa's first draft of De occulta philosophia, sent to Trithemius
letters.value: Not established whether it holds any of the alphabets
letters.form: Agrippa stayed with Trithemius at Würzburg ('conversant with you in your Monastery of Herbipolis', 1651 letter) and afterwards sent him a draft of his book on occult philosophy 'by this bearer', with a dedicatory letter. Trithemius received it shortly before 8 April 1510. His reply, praising it and advising him to share such things only with fit friends, is dated 'Ex nostro coenobio Peapolitano. VIII. die Aprilis' in the 1533 print and 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' in the 1651 English. The draft survives at Würzburg. Agrippa's own 'To the Reader' says that for the print 'we added some Chapters'. Vittoria Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Leiden: Brill, 1992) takes account of the Würzburg manuscript and is the place to settle the question; how it presents the draft was not checked.

letters.name: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia libri tres
letters.value: Theban (III.29); Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii in one woodcut (III.30); the nine chambers (III.30); the planetary squares, seals and characters (II.22); the geomantic characters (II.51)
letters.form: The book through which nearly every later reader met the magical alphabets. Book III, chapter 29 ('De characteribus & sigillis spirituum' in the 1533 contents; 'Of the Characters and Seals of spirits' in J.F.'s English of 1651) gives the Theban as characters 'quos notat Petrus Apponus ab Honorio Thebano traditos'. Its table is labelled A–Z and ends in a sign with a small ω, labelled ω. Chapter 30 ('Alius characterizandi modus, à Cabalistis traditus') says that among the Hebrews there are several fashions of characters. The most ancient is that of Moses and the prophets. It then names three more in two sentences: the Celestial, 'because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars'; the Malachim, 'of Angels, or Regal'; and 'the passing through the River' (J.F. 1651, p. 439). They follow as three separately captioned tables. 'Scriptura Coelestis' (22 signs in rows of 9, 9 and 4) stands on p. CCLXXIII, with the caption 'Scriptura Malachim' at the foot of the page. The Malachim (23 signs, two of them labelled Samech) and 'Scriptura transitus fluuii' (22 signs in rows of 8, 7 and 7) follow on p. CCLXXIIII. The same chapter gives the nine-chamber cipher. Book II, chapter 22 gives the planetary tables with their seals and characters. II.48 and II.51 give the geomantic figures and the characters drawn from them, and II.51 calls the Malachim the true characters of the heavens.

letters.form: A short primer of twelve alphabets with brief rules for reading each. A secondary source seen only in a search summary reports that Ambrogio tells of a script said to be in a demon's own hand, after one Lodovico de Spoletano conjured the demon. In III.30 Agrippa gives that origin to the Celestial, but in II.51 he calls the Malachim itself 'the true Characters of the heavens', so Mathers has ground in Agrippa. Mathers reads the inscription of the Sixth Pentacle of Mars (Figure 30), 'Elohim qeber, Elohim hath covered (or protected)', as written in 'the Secret Alphabet of Malachim'. On the pentacle of Plate III, six of the nine orders of angels are named in ordinary Hebrew and the rest in the Passing of the River. Plate XV ('The Mystical Alphabets') prints the alphabet he calls the 'Alphabet of the Magi', the earliest use of that English name found.

Later printings used new cuts or engravings (1550, 1561, 1651, Duret 1613, Barrett 1801), and the 1533 issues themselves vary. A drawing must name the edition it follows. Barrett's plate follows the English of 1651 at a remove from 1533.
Never write 'Honorius of Thebes invented the Theban' or 'Agrippa invented the Celestial'. Write 'Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius of Thebes' and 'Agrippa presents them as writings of the Hebrews'.
Do not date the Hebrew-keyed alphabets to 1510 (the draft) or to 1531 (Book I only). The first documented printing of III.29–30 is July 1533.
Do not call Agrippa Trithemius's pupil. The documented contact is the visit of 1509–10 and the letter of 8 April 1510.
The River script was printed in 1523 (de Balmes) and 1530 (Panteo) before Agrippa. Agrippa does not cite de Balmes; the pointer to de Balmes is Peterson's editorial note.
Postel's 1538 primer holds real alphabets, not magical ones, as far as this research knows. Do not present it as a grimoire.
